entries.title: Deuteronomy 5:1
segments: The great object of attending to and becoming acquianted with the laws of God should be, that we may obey them.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 5:3
segments: Our fathers; Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 5:6
segments: The Lord ever speaks to his people as if their deliverance from bondage was a great and precious blessing, and one which laid them under new and peculiar obligations to love and serve him.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 5:8
segments: Any graven image, or any likeness; to bow down to, adore, or worship.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 5:14
segments: Servants as well as masters have an inalienable right, and it is their indispensable duty, to rest from their labors on the Sabbath, and to keep it holy: masters are sacredly bound to grant servants liberty and opportunity for this.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 5:15
segments: Therefore the Lord--commanded; this was to the Israelites a reason, in addition to that mentioned,

, why they should keep the Sabbath; and especially why their servants should enjoy its rest and privileges. 
 
The giving of a new reason why men should perform a duty, is no evidence that the duty was not binding before that reason was given or even existed; or that there are not many other reasons for the performance of the duty.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 5:16
segments: Few duties are more intimately connected with or essential to the prosperity of children, than a kind, affectionate, hearty obedience to their parents.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 5:21
segments: It is wrong not only to take what we ought not to have, but even to desire it.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 5:22
segments: The obligations expressed in the ten commands, which were written by God on tables of stone, are moral: they arise from the nature of men, and their relations to God and their fellow men; and are binding upon all who know them, in all ages and in all countries.

entries.title: Deuteronomy 5:33
segments: Obedience to all the commands of God is conducive to the highest good of men, in this world as well as in the world to come.
